Course overview

Short Stories

Read across Short Fiction, Drama and Suspense and Poetry and Song. Use the course lessons to build a shared language for evidence, interpretation, and response.

I can...

  • explain how literary choices shape meaning.
  • support an interpretation with precise textual evidence.
  • compare how different texts develop perspective, conflict, and theme.
  • plan a clear personal, critical, or creative response.

Reading and responding

Audience

The intended reader, listener, or viewer whose knowledge, expectations, and needs shape a text or response.

Word structure or origin
The Latin root aud- means “hear.” Audience originally named a group that hears something and now includes readers and viewers.
Related terms
reader, listener, viewer, intended audience
Where this appears
Writing a Short Story Analysis and the Critical Essay guide
Compare with the course model

Course source: Critical Essay and Writing a Short Story Analysis guides

A critical essay assumes a reader who needs the text, context, claim, and evidence explained. Naming a detail without explaining how it supports the interpretation leaves that audience to make the connection alone.

Responses save automatically

Reading and responding

Purpose

The reason a text or response is created, such as to entertain, inform, persuade, reflect, or analyze.

Word structure or origin
Purpose is a whole borrowed word in English. In this course, it names what a writer is trying to accomplish.
Related terms
intention, goal, function, effect
Where this appears
What Do Good Readers Do? and the writing guides
Compare with the course model

Course source: Writing a Short Story Analysis

The purpose of analysis is not to retell the plot. It is to explain how a specific literary choice works and why that choice matters to the meaning of the text.

Responses save automatically

Reading and responding

Context

The surrounding historical, cultural, social, or textual information that helps a reader understand a choice or idea.

Word structure or origin
Con- means “together,” and the root related to text means “woven.” Context is what is woven together around a detail.
Related terms
background, situation, circumstances, setting
Where this appears
Harrison Bergeron and the Critical Essay guide
Compare with the course model

Course source: Harrison Bergeron

The story’s year, laws, and government-controlled handicaps create the context for its exaggerated version of equality. Without that frame, Harrison’s rebellion would lose much of its satirical meaning.

Responses save automatically

Reading and responding

Annotation

A purposeful note, mark, question, or connection added while reading to record thinking and support later interpretation.

Word structure or origin
Ad- means “toward,” not- means “mark,” and -ation names a process: the process of adding a mark or note.
Related terms
annotate, margin note, close reading, active reading
Where this appears
What Do Good Readers Do? and its annotation material
Compare with the course model

Course source: What Do Good Readers Do? and annotation guidance

A useful annotation beside a turning point might identify an unfamiliar word, record a prediction, and ask why a character made that choice. Merely highlighting an entire paragraph does not preserve the reader’s thinking.

Responses save automatically

Reading and responding

Inference

A reasonable conclusion reached by combining textual clues with relevant prior knowledge rather than relying on a direct statement.

Word structure or origin
In- means “into,” the root fer means “carry,” and -ence names a result: a conclusion carried from the evidence.
Related terms
infer, implication, clue, conclusion
Where this appears
The Cask of Amontillado and the reading-strategy lesson
Compare with the course model

Course source: The Cask of Amontillado

Montresor’s careful manipulation of Fortunato and his vague account of the original injury support the inference that his version of justice is not trustworthy. The story does not state that conclusion directly.

Responses save automatically

Reading and responding

Interpretation

An evidence-supported explanation of what a text means or suggests; more than one interpretation may be reasonable.

Word structure or origin
Interpret means to explain meaning, and -ation names the process or result of doing so.
Related terms
reading, explanation, meaning, perspective
Where this appears
I Am a Rock and Topic and Interpretation
Compare with the course model

Course source: I Am a Rock

The repeated images of isolation support an interpretation that the speaker uses emotional distance as protection. The insistence on being unaffected may also reveal the vulnerability the speaker is trying to hide.

Responses save automatically

Reading and responding

Textual Evidence

A precise quotation, action, image, structural choice, or other detail from a text used to support an inference or claim.

Word structure or origin
Text is joined to -ual, meaning “related to.” Evidence comes from a root meaning “to see clearly.”
Related terms
quotation, detail, proof, support, citation
Where this appears
Personal Response: Text Evidence and every question set
Compare with the course model

Course source: The Flying Machine

The Emperor’s decision to destroy the machine and its inventor is a precise action that can support a claim about fear, power, or responsibility. Saying only that “something bad happens” is too vague to function as evidence.

Responses save automatically

Reading and responding

Analysis

The explanation of how a textual choice works, why it matters, and how it develops a larger idea.

Word structure or origin
The Greek parts behind analysis suggest “loosening apart.” Analysis separates a text into choices so their relationships can be understood.
Related terms
analyze, examine, explain, significance
Where this appears
Writing a Short Story Analysis and the Analysis Explorer
Compare with the course model

Course source: Harrison Bergeron

The handicaps do more than identify the society’s rules. Their exaggerated effects expose how the government confuses equal human worth with forced sameness, which develops the story’s criticism of authoritarian control.

Responses save automatically

Reading and responding

Summary

A concise, accurate account of a text’s central situation, key developments, and outcome without extended interpretation.

Word structure or origin
Sum means “total,” and -ary means “related to.” A summary gives the essential total in a shortened form.
Related terms
summarize, central idea, key event, retell
Where this appears
Reading Short Stories and all five readings
Compare with the course model

Course source: Flight into Danger

After an in-flight emergency incapacitates the crew, people aboard the aircraft must rely on a passenger with past flying experience and support from the ground to attempt a safe landing. This states the central situation without explaining a theme.

Responses save automatically

Reading and responding

Synthesis

The creation of a larger insight by combining ideas, evidence, or patterns from more than one part or text.

Word structure or origin
The Greek part syn- means “together,” and thesis means “placing.” Synthesis places ideas together to create something new.
Related terms
combine, connect, compare, integrate
Where this appears
The course overview, Critical Essay guide, and cross-text writing tasks
Compare with the course model

Course sources: The Cask of Amontillado and Harrison Bergeron

Both texts show people justifying cruelty through a stated principle—revenge in one and enforced equality in the other. Read together, they suggest that a principle can become dangerous when power removes accountability.

Responses save automatically

Reading and responding

Claim

A focused, arguable statement about a text that requires relevant evidence and reasoning.

Word structure or origin
Claim functions as a whole root word in English; it names an assertion a writer is prepared to support.
Related terms
assertion, position, argument, reason
Where this appears
The Critical Essay body lessons and Writing Studio
Compare with the course model

Course source: The Flying Machine

The Emperor’s response shows that fear of possible misuse can turn an attempt to protect society into an act of oppression. This is arguable and can be tested against his choices in the story.

Responses save automatically

Reading and responding

Thesis / Controlling Idea

The central, arguable idea that directs a response and gives its evidence and paragraphs a shared purpose.

Word structure or origin
Thesis comes from a Greek word meaning “a placing” or proposition. A controlling idea is the idea placed at the centre of the response.
Related terms
central argument, controlling idea, position, line of reasoning
Where this appears
Topic and Interpretation and Personal Response planning
Compare with the course model

Course source: The Cask of Amontillado and the Critical Essay guide

Through Montresor’s controlled first-person narration, dramatic irony, and the confined catacomb setting, Poe shows how wounded pride can turn revenge into deliberate cruelty. Each named choice can organize a body paragraph.

Responses save automatically

Reading and responding

Form and Structure

Form is the kind or shape of a text; structure is the deliberate arrangement of its parts and their relationships.

Word structure or origin
Form means “shape.” The root struct means “build,” and -ure names the result: structure is how a text is built.
Related terms
organization, sequence, pattern, prose, poetry, song
Where this appears
Prose Form and Perspective and all five texts
Compare with the course model

Course source: I Am a Rock

The song form uses repeated declarations and a returning refrain. That circular structure makes the speaker’s defence sound practiced and persistent, unlike a prose narrative that moves through a sequence of events.

Responses save automatically

Reading and responding

Revision

The process of re-seeing and substantially improving ideas, organization, evidence, and explanation—not only correcting surface errors.

Word structure or origin
Re- means “again,” vis means “see,” and -ion names a process. Revision literally means seeing again.
Related terms
rework, reorganize, clarify, edit, proofread
Where this appears
Conclusion and Revision and Draft and Revise
Compare with the course model

Course source: Conclusion and Revision guide

Changing “This story is good because it has symbolism” into a focused statement that names the symbol, its pattern, and the idea it develops is revision. Correcting one comma in the original sentence is editing, not re-seeing the analysis.

Responses save automatically

Story form and structure

Genre

A recognizable kind of text with shared forms, purposes, conventions, and reader expectations.

Word structure or origin
The French word genre means “kind” or “type.” It is used as a whole borrowed word in English.
Related terms
short story, drama, poetry, song, dystopia, satire
Where this appears
Short Story Bank groupings and Literary Terms Review
Compare with the course model

Course source: Harrison Bergeron

The story uses a future society and exaggerated government control, so reading it as dystopian satire prepares us to look for criticism rather than treating its world as a realistic prediction.

Responses save automatically

Story form and structure

Narrative / Narrator

A narrative is an organized account of events; the narrator is the constructed voice that presents that account to the reader.

Word structure or origin
The root narrat- means “tell.” -ive forms a thing or quality, while -or names the one who performs the action.
Related terms
story, narration, storyteller, speaker
Where this appears
Short Story Terms and the five readings
Compare with the course model

Course source: The Cask of Amontillado

Montresor is the first-person narrator, not Edgar Allan Poe. His control over what is explained, omitted, and justified shapes the entire revenge narrative and requires readers to question his reliability.

Responses save automatically

Story form and structure

Plot Structure

The causal arrangement of a story’s major events, often described through exposition, an initial or inciting incident, rising action, climax, falling action, and resolution or denouement.

Word structure or origin
Plot is a whole root word. The root struct means “build,” so plot structure describes how events are built into a sequence.
Related terms
exposition, inciting incident, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution, denouement
Where this appears
Short Story Terms and the Elements Workbench
Compare with the course model

Course source: The Cask of Amontillado

The carnival encounter establishes Montresor’s plan, the descent and wine search intensify danger, the chaining and walling form the decisive crisis, and the later reflection closes the account. Each stage advances the revenge plot.

Responses save automatically

Story form and structure

Ending Types

Ways a text closes its action or meaning, including explicit, implicit, twist, unresolved, and tie-back endings.

Word structure or origin
Ending combines end with -ing. Type comes from a word for an impression or model used to classify patterns.
Related terms
explicit, implicit, twist, unresolved, tie-back, resolution
Where this appears
The Endings section in Short Story Terms
Compare with the course model

Course source: The Flying Machine

The immediate plot is resolved when the Emperor eliminates the invention and inventor, but the ethical question remains open: has he protected his people or committed an injustice? The action is explicit while the judgment is not.

Responses save automatically

Story form and structure

Flashback

A shift from a narrative’s current time to an earlier event in order to reveal information, motivation, or contrast.

Word structure or origin
A transparent compound: flash suggests a sudden view, and back signals movement to an earlier time.
Related terms
retrospective narration, chronology, memory, time shift
Where this appears
Short Story Terms and The Cask of Amontillado
Compare with the course model

Course source: The Cask of Amontillado

Montresor recounts a crime from many years earlier. The whole story uses a retrospective frame; that is different from a brief flashback inserted into an otherwise present-time narrative, but both ask why the past is being revealed now.

Responses save automatically

Story form and structure

Foreshadowing

A clue or pattern that prepares readers for a later event without fully revealing what will happen.

Word structure or origin
Fore- means “before,” shadow suggests an outline, and -ing names the action: casting an outline before the event.
Related terms
hint, clue, prediction, anticipation
Where this appears
Short Story Terms and the suspense texts in the Story Bank
Compare with the course model

Course source: The Cask of Amontillado

Montresor’s repeated concern about the damp catacombs sounds courteous, but it keeps death and danger in view. His possession of a mason’s trowel becomes an even sharper clue once the reader understands his plan.

Story form and structure

Suspense / Pacing

Suspense is anxious uncertainty about what will happen; pacing is the rate at which information and events are delivered to create that experience.

Word structure or origin
The root pend in suspense means “hang,” as if the outcome is hanging. Pacing comes from pace, the rate of movement.
Related terms
tension, delay, urgency, tempo, reveal
Where this appears
Flight into Danger and Reading Short Stories
Compare with the course model

Course source: Flight into Danger

The emergency unfolds through urgent decisions, limited time, and staged preparations for landing. The text controls what can be solved at each step, so the approaching landing becomes a deadline that drives both pacing and suspense.

Responses save automatically

Story form and structure

Setting

The time, place, physical environment, and social conditions in which a text’s action occurs.

Word structure or origin
Set means to place, and -ing forms a noun for the surrounding placement of the action.
Related terms
time, place, environment, social setting, atmosphere
Where this appears
The Setting section in Short Story Terms and the Analysis Explorer
Compare with the course model

Course source: The Cask of Amontillado

The movement from a crowded carnival to dark, confined catacombs isolates Fortunato and gives Montresor control. The contrast makes the setting part of the trap rather than a neutral backdrop.

Story form and structure

Dialogue

Spoken exchange between characters, shaped to reveal information, relationships, conflict, or changes in action.

Word structure or origin
The Greek parts dia- and logos suggest meaning moving through speech or discourse.
Related terms
conversation, speech, exchange, subtext

Compare with the course model

Course source: Flight into Danger

The urgent exchanges between the aircraft and people providing support carry technical information while exposing fear, responsibility, and trust. The dialogue advances the emergency rather than pausing it.

Character, conflict, and perspective

Protagonist

The central character whose goals, choices, and conflicts organize the main action; a protagonist is not automatically heroic or morally right.

Word structure or origin
The Greek part proto- means “first,” and agon means “contest” or competitor: the first or central participant in the struggle.
Related terms
central character, main character, goal, agency
Where this appears
The Characters section in Short Story Terms
Compare with the course model

Course source: Harrison Bergeron

Harrison functions as the central challenger during the story’s decisive action because his attempt to reject the handicaps brings the conflict with the government into the open. Calling him the protagonist does not settle whether every choice he makes is wise.

Responses save automatically

Character, conflict, and perspective

Antagonist

The character, institution, force, or internal pressure that blocks the protagonist’s goal and drives the central conflict.

Word structure or origin
Anti- means “against,” and agon means “contest” or competitor: the force positioned against the central goal.
Related terms
opposition, obstacle, force, adversary
Where this appears
Short Story Terms, the Characters workbench, and Conflict
Compare with the course model

Course source: Harrison Bergeron

The government’s system of enforced handicaps is the main antagonistic force. Diana Moon Glampers acts for that system, but the opposition is larger than one individual because law, media, and punishment all maintain it.

Responses save automatically

Character, conflict, and perspective

Character Traits / Motivation

Traits are relatively stable qualities shown through behaviour; motivation is the need, value, fear, or desire that helps explain a character’s choices.

Word structure or origin
Trait is a whole borrowed word. Motiv- is related to movement, and -ation names the process that moves a character to act.
Related terms
motive, desire, fear, value, behaviour, goal
Where this appears
The Characters workbench, Story Questions, and Analysis Explorer
Compare with the course model

Course source: The Cask of Amontillado

Montresor’s planning, patience, and ability to imitate concern reveal calculation. His stated motivation is revenge for an insult to his pride, although the lack of a clear offence makes that motive questionable rather than automatically justified.

Responses save automatically

Character, conflict, and perspective

Characterization

The methods a writer uses to develop a character directly through description or indirectly through speech, thoughts, actions, appearance, and effects on others.

Word structure or origin
Character joins -ize, “make or present as,” and -ation, a process: the process of constructing a character.
Related terms
direct, indirect, speech, thoughts, actions, effects
Where this appears
The Characters workbench and Analysis Explorer
Compare with the course model

Course source: Harrison Bergeron

Descriptions of Harrison’s extreme handicaps directly establish how the government labels his abilities. His decision to tear them away and challenge the broadcast indirectly characterizes his confidence, defiance, and desire for freedom.

Character, conflict, and perspective

Character Types / Character Arc

Character types describe complexity and change—round, flat, static, dynamic, stereotyped, or foil—while an arc traces how a character’s understanding or behaviour develops.

Word structure or origin
Character comes from a word for an identifying mark. An arc is a curved path, used figuratively for development across a text.
Related terms
round, flat, static, dynamic, stereotyped, foil, development
Where this appears
The Characters section and Character Workbench in Short Story Terms
Compare with the course model

Course sources: Character Workbench and the unit readings

Montresor remains largely static in his commitment to revenge, while the person forced to respond to the crisis in Flight into Danger must move from reluctance and uncertainty toward action. A character arc requires evidence from more than one point in the text.

Character, conflict, and perspective

Conflict

A struggle between opposing wants, values, forces, or conditions; conflict may be internal or external, including person versus person, self, society, or environment.

Word structure or origin
Con- means “together,” and the root flict means “strike.” Conflict brings forces into collision.
Related terms
internal, external, person vs. person, self, society, environment
Where this appears
The Conflict section in Short Story Terms and the Analysis Explorer
Compare with the course model

Course source: Harrison Bergeron

Harrison’s central external conflict is person versus society because he resists a system that limits ability through law and force. His struggle with individual enforcers is part of that larger institutional conflict.

Responses save automatically

Character, conflict, and perspective

Point of View / Narrative Perspective

The position from which a text is told and the limits placed on what can be known, including first person, third-person limited, omniscient, and objective perspectives.

Word structure or origin
Point of view is a phrase for a viewing position. In perspective, roots meaning “through” and “look” emphasize the lens through which events are seen.
Related terms
first person, third-person limited, omniscient, objective, reliability
Where this appears
Short Story Terms, Literary Terms Review, and the Analysis Explorer
Compare with the course model

Course source: The Cask of Amontillado

First-person narration limits the account to Montresor’s words and judgments. Readers see his plan clearly but never receive Fortunato’s inner perspective or independent proof that the original offence deserved revenge.

Character, conflict, and perspective

Archetype

A recurring character, situation, image, or journey pattern that readers recognize across many stories and cultures.

Word structure or origin
The Greek part arche- means “original” or “beginning,” and type means a pattern or model.
Related terms
hero, mentor, outsider, journey, test, recurring pattern
Where this appears
Literary Terms Review and the unit readings
Compare with the course model

Course source: Flight into Danger

The passenger called on to use past experience during a crisis fits a reluctant-hero pattern: an ordinary journey becomes a test that requires action despite fear. The archetype helps compare stories without erasing this text’s specific details.

Style and meaning

Voice / Style

Voice is the distinctive presence created by a speaker or narrator; style is the broader pattern of language, structure, and technique that creates that presence and effect.

Word structure or origin
Voice comes from a root related to speech. Style comes from stylus, a writing tool, and now names a characteristic way of writing.
Related terms
speaker, narrator, diction, syntax, rhythm, register
Where this appears
I Am a Rock and Personal Response
Compare with the course model

Course source: I Am a Rock

The speaker’s voice is controlled and defensive, built through repeated first-person declarations and firm images of separation. The repetition makes the style sound like a belief the speaker is trying to maintain.

Responses save automatically

Style and meaning

Tone

The attitude a speaker, narrator, or writer creates toward a subject, character, situation, or audience through language choices.

Word structure or origin
Tone comes from a Greek word related to tension or sound. In reading, it names the attitudinal quality carried by the language.
Related terms
attitude, stance, voice, diction, formal, bitter, playful
Where this appears
Literary Terms Review and the Analysis Explorer
Compare with the course model

Course source: The Cask of Amontillado

Montresor’s orderly account and polite performance create a cold, controlled tone. That calmness makes the planned violence more disturbing because the narrator rarely sounds uncertain or remorseful.

Responses save automatically

Style and meaning

Mood / Atmosphere

The emotional experience or surrounding feeling a text creates for readers through setting, imagery, pacing, sound, and detail.

Word structure or origin
Mood is a whole root word. In atmosphere, Greek roots for “vapour” and “sphere” suggest the environment surrounding an experience.
Related terms
feeling, tension, environment, eerie, hopeful, claustrophobic
Where this appears
Literary Terms Review, Setting, and the Analysis Explorer
Compare with the course model

Course source: The Cask of Amontillado

The bright public carnival gives way to damp underground chambers, narrowing movement and light. That shift creates an increasingly claustrophobic and threatening atmosphere for the reader.

Style and meaning

Diction / Syntax

Diction is deliberate word choice; syntax is the arrangement of words, phrases, and sentences. Together they shape clarity, rhythm, tone, and emphasis.

Word structure or origin
The root dict means “say,” and -ion names the result. Greek parts in syntax mean “arrange together.”
Related terms
word choice, sentence structure, register, rhythm, emphasis

Literary Terms Review, Personal Response, and every course text
Compare with the course model

Course source: Flight into Danger

Direct vocabulary and short exchanges keep attention on immediate decisions during the emergency. The compressed syntax accelerates the scene and makes each instruction feel consequential.

Style and meaning

Imagery

Language that appeals to sight, sound, touch, taste, smell, or bodily sensation to create a concrete experience or pattern of meaning.

Word structure or origin
Image joins -ry, a suffix that can name a collection or practice: imagery is a text’s system of sensory images.
Related terms
sensory detail, visual, auditory, tactile, image pattern

Compare with the course model

Course source: I Am a Rock

The winter, wall, rock, and island images make emotional isolation physical and visible. Because the images recur, they do more than decorate the song; they build the speaker’s defensive world.

Style and meaning

Figurative Language

Language whose intended meaning extends beyond the literal, including metaphor, simile, personification, and hyperbole.

Word structure or origin
Figure means a shape or representation, and -ative means “related to.” A metaphor carries meaning across concepts; a simile signals likeness.
Related terms
metaphor, simile, personification, hyperbole, comparison

Compare with the course model

Course source: I Am a Rock

Style and meaning

Alliteration

The deliberate repetition of initial consonant sounds in nearby stressed words to create emphasis, rhythm, connection, or sound effect.

Word structure or origin
The word developed from Latin roots related to “toward” and “letter.” The important feature is repeated sound, not merely repeated spelling.
Related terms
consonance, sound device, repetition, rhythm
Where this appears
Literary Terms Review and poetry or song analysis
Compare with the course model

Course source: I Am a Rock

The clustered initial s sounds in the song’s winter and snow imagery soften and slow the passage. The sound pattern helps deepen the quiet sense of isolation rather than functioning as decoration alone.

Responses save automatically

Style and meaning

Symbolism / Motif

A symbol is a concrete detail that carries meaning beyond itself; a motif is a recurring element whose pattern helps develop a larger idea.

Word structure or origin
Greek roots in symbol mean “throw together,” joining a thing with an idea. -ism forms a practice; motif names a recurring design.
Related terms
symbol, motif, recurring image, pattern, association
Where this appears
Literary Terms Review, Short Story Terms, and the Analysis Explorer
Compare with the course model

Course source: The Cask of Amontillado

The wine motif repeatedly draws on Fortunato’s pride and moves him deeper into the trap. The wall becomes more than masonry: it makes Montresor’s desire to control, silence, and permanently contain his victim concrete.

Style and meaning

Irony

A meaningful gap between words and intent, expectation and outcome, or a character’s knowledge and the audience’s knowledge.

Word structure or origin
Irony comes through Greek and originally involved a speaker who conceals or understates meaning. Course analysis distinguishes verbal, situational, and dramatic forms.
Related terms
verbal, situational, dramatic, expectation, reversal
Where this appears
Literary Terms Review and the Analysis Explorer
Compare with the course model

Course source: The Cask of Amontillado

Readers know that Montresor is pursuing revenge while Fortunato believes he is being led to inspect wine. That knowledge gap creates dramatic irony in Montresor’s apparently friendly words and warnings.

Responses save automatically

Style and meaning

Satire

The use of humour, irony, exaggeration, or absurdity to expose and criticize human behaviour, institutions, or social ideas.

Word structure or origin
Satire is a whole borrowed word, associated with a Latin term for a mixed dish. The form combines techniques to sharpen criticism.
Related terms
exaggeration, ridicule, irony, parody, social criticism

Literary Terms Review and Harrison Bergeron
Compare with the course model

Course source: Harrison Bergeron

The absurdly heavy and disruptive handicaps exaggerate a policy of forced sameness. The exaggeration exposes how an ideal can be distorted when a government treats excellence and individuality as threats.

Style and meaning

Allusion

A brief, indirect reference to a known person, event, place, story, artwork, or tradition that depends on shared knowledge.

Word structure or origin
Allude means to refer indirectly, and -sion forms the noun for that act or result.
Related terms
reference, mythology, history, culture, shared knowledge

Course source: Literary Terms Review

An allusion should point to a recognizable outside person, event, story, or tradition and add meaning through that reference. A general resemblance between Harrison Bergeron and another dystopia is a comparison, not automatically proof of an allusion.

Juxtaposition

The deliberate placement of two characters, images, settings, or ideas beside one another so their contrast or relationship becomes clearer.

Word structure or origin
The Latin part juxta means “beside,” and position means placement: placing elements beside one another.
Related terms
contrast, comparison, side by side, foil, parallel

Style and meaning

Ambiguity

Deliberate uncertainty or openness that allows more than one defensible meaning, motive, or outcome.

Word structure or origin
Ambi- means “both” or “around,” and -ity names a quality: the quality of allowing more than one direction of meaning.
Related terms
uncertainty, open-endedness, multiple meanings, unresolved

Style and meaning

Theme / Thematic Statement

Theme is a developed insight about human experience; a thematic statement expresses that insight as a complete idea, while thematic complexity recognizes tensions or limits within it.

Word structure or origin
Theme comes from a Greek word for “something placed.” Thematic adds “related to,” and a statement places the idea into a complete claim.
Related terms
topic, thematic statement, insight, message, complexity
Where this appears
Short Story Terms, Literary Terms Review, and the Analysis Explorer

What Do Good Readers Do?

Short Stories Introduction

You read for many different reasons, you read for entertainment, for information, and to learn. Sometimes reading is fun, but sometimes it's hard work.  Reading is an active process. Think of it as a conversation between you - your thoughts, questions and experiences - and the words on the page

Below are 4 stages in the reading process, with some suggested activities for each stage. You can decide which activities would be most helpful for each reading task you undertake.

Stages in the Reading Process

1. Before Reading

Get to know the selection you are going to read.

2. Reading

Dive in and read through the text.

3. Rereading

Get more out of what you have read: to clarify your understanding of it and to gather information for class assignments.

4. After Reading

Reflect on what you've read, to show your understanding of it, and to use the information in a creative way.

1. Before Reading

Look over the text you are going to read and use some of the following strategies to get an idea of what it is like.

  • make predictions based on the title, the name of the author, and any other works or illustrations included
  • read any headings, subheadings, and captions
  • ask questions about the topic
  • examine any maps, photographs, graphs, charts, tables, illustrations, and pictures
  • skim the table of contents and select the chapters or sections you find most interesting or useful
  • recall what you already know about the subject or content

2. Reading 

As you read, think about your own responses to the material using some of these strategies.

  • just read and enjoy
  • keep a reading journal
  • think about or take notes on what you've read
  • ask questions about anything you don't understand or don't agree with
  • list words you don't know and look up their definitions
  • discuss your responses to the selection with other readers
  • make connections to what you know already or have read elsewhere
  • pay attention to any pictures or images you think of as you read

***many of these are done when annotating the text you read


3. Rereading

At this stage, you might:

  • read the selection aloud, either to yourself or to others
  • review the selection again to fill in gaps in your notes
  • create webs, charts, graphs, and other diagrams to organize information
  • discuss questions about the selection with a partner


After Reading

You might:

  • make a follow-up entry in your reading journal
  • write an essay or prepare an oral presentation about the selection, or use information from the selection in an essay or report
  • answer any questions or do any activities included with the selection
  • discuss the selection with someone else
  • review any notes you made while reading and revise them where necessary (annotations)
The reading process is not a set of rules; it is a set of possibilities.  You don't follow the same steps in the same order every time you read. You may read the same selection in different ways, depending on your reason for reading it. For example, if you read a novel for your enjoyment, you may read it very quickly. But if you have to write an essay about a novel, you may read it more slowly and carefully.

Lesson 2: Storytelling

Storytelling

Introduction to Storytelling

Imagine a world without books, televisions, radios or computers. How could people share their knowledge, and record their history? What would they do to pass the time - especially during the long evening hours? How would they entertain themselves and each other? The answer to these questions is obvious: they would tell stories.

The History of Storytelling
Storytelling is one of the oldest forms of human communication. Long before books or writing, people shared knowledge, beliefs, and traditions through spoken stories. These stories helped explain natural events, taught lessons, and preserved cultural history. From cave paintings to myths passed down through generations, storytelling has always been a way for communities to connect and remember who they are.

The Importance of Storytelling
Storytelling continues to be important today because it shapes how we understand the world and each other. Stories teach values, spark imagination, and allow us to experience different perspectives. They help us connect across cultures and time, making sure knowledge, traditions, and emotions are carried forward. Whether told aloud, written, or shown in films, storytelling is a powerful tool for communication and learning.

Lesson 3: Reading Short Stories

Reading Short Stories

The following information will assist you with being prepared to read short stories.

What is a Short Story?

A short story is a brief tale written to entertain you and keep you turning the pages to find how it ends. Reading a short story is like taking a trip to a new place inhabited by people you have never met. Short-story authors write to tell you their ideas about people and the world.  By sharing the lives of fictional characters, you gain insights into human nature and behaviour. You may also learn something about yourself.

The Elements of a Short Story

A short-story writer quickly pulls you into the lives of the characters and makes you care about their feelings, their relationships, and their problems.  Every detail and event in a short story is carefully chosen by the writer to contribute to the overall effect. Here are some o the elements used in writing a short story.

Characters

Believable, interesting characters that you care about are at the heart of a good short story. Be alert to how the main characters grow and change through the events in the story.

Setting

The setting is the tine and place in which the story takes place,  The setting often tells you something about the characters and helps to create the atmosphere or mood.

Conflict

Challenges, conflict, or struggle are the basis of every story. Characters may struggle with other people, with animals, with forces of nature or with something inside themselves.

Point of View

Every story is told from a particular point of view. It may be told from the point of view of one character in the story, or from the point of view of a narrator who knows and sees everything.

Plot

The plot is the chain of events in a story. Many stories follow a pattern: the author establishes the characters the setting and the conflict, and then adds complications. The climax is the turning point of the story where the conflict is resolved and the loose ends are tied up.

Suspense

Suspense is what makes you worry about the characters and what will become of them.  A life-threatening situation, for example, makes for a  suspenseful story.

Theme

The theme is the main idea in a story. It is what the story has to say about life and human nature. Keep in mind that different readers may interpret the same story in quite different ways.

How to Read a Short Story

Here are some strategies you can use to get the most from reading a short story.

1. Ease into the story

Before you begin to read a story, take some time to get ready.

  • Read the title and think about what might happen in the story.
  • Do you know this author? If so, what kind of story might this be?
  • Look at any illustrations. what do they tell you about the story?
  • Read the first page of the story and pause. What do you know so far about the characters, setting, conflict, and point of view? Where do you think the story is going?

2. Get involved in the story

The key to being a good reader is being an active reader. Here are some of the things you can do to be an active reader.

  • ask questions about what is happening
  • make predictions about what might happen next.
  • put yourself in the characters' shoes.
  • form opinions about what is going on.
  • think about your responses to what you are reading.
  • picture the setting and events in your mind, or even draw them!
  • write down your favourite quotations from the story.
  • make connections to what you already know.

3. Write about the story

Making notes can help you focus your thinking as you read. Here are some ways of writing about a story.

  • use a response journal to record your thoughts about the story
  • take notes or draw webs to keep track of the characters and events in a complex story.
  • sketch the setting of the story, or draw a map.

Lesson 4: Short Story Terms

Elements of Fiction

Review the following terms:

Antagonist

is the character or force that is trying to stop the protagonist from achieving his goals.

Characters

are the people in the story. There are different types of characters.

Climax

the point in the story where we find out if the protagonist wins or loses. It is the most exciting point of any story.

Conflict

is the problem facing the protagonist. It is what he is trying to overcome. The three main conflicts are: Person vs Person, Person vs Environment, and Person vs Him/her/themself.

Exposition

can be considered the introduction of the short story. We usually learn of the setting and are introduced to the major characters.

Falling Action

 any thing that happens after the climax.

Flat Character

is a character with only one or two characteristics. We don’t know much about them.

Genre

in literature, this means “type”.

Initial Incident

is the first thing that happens that makes us go ‘I wonder what is going to happen next’.

Plot

is the sequence of events that makes up a story. It is ‘what happens’. The plot has several sub sections.

Point of View

refers to the way the author tells the story and how the ‘reader’ sees it.

First Person Point of View - the author is a character in the story and uses ‘I’.  Ex. When John walked into the room, I was amazed.

Third Person Narrative - the author uses he/she but only exists in one character’s mind. Ex.  When John walked into the room, she was amazed.
Third Person Omniscient - the author can be in the mind of any character.  Ex. When John walked into the room, she was amazed but Jim was angry.

Protagonist

is a major character who is trying to achieve a goal. Usually he is the character we are ‘rooting for’.

Rising Action

the series of problems protagonists face as they pursue their goal.

Round Character

is a character with many personality traits. He is a complete person. The protagonist is always a round character.

Setting

 is the ‘time and place’ of the story. It has a great impact on the ‘feeling’ of the story and how the reader reacts to it.

Stereotyped Character

is a character who is seen in many similar ways in different stories - the brave knight - the damsel in distress - the dumb blond, etc.

Theme

is the message of the story. It is not the plot; it is what the plot is trying to show. Sometimes you can figure out the theme by asking, "what is the author trying to tells us about ... (relationships/identity/betrayal/ambition etc.)"

Point of View Definitions: Point of View a particular attitude or way of considering a matter.
Writers use a range of techniques and devices to create the effects they’re after.
Annotate important passages as you read.

Characters

Characterization-the author's method of developing the character so that we understand what he or she is like. Writers have many ways in which to develop the character.

Direct Characterization refers to characterization methods by which the writer directly tells us what the character is like. This is done via direct statements by the writer regarding the personality of the character.

Indirect Characterization refers to the other ways in which an author might reveal a character. We come to understand something about characters by reading about their thoughts, words, and deeds. We also learn about characters based on what other characters say or think about them. Finally, we can learn about a character's personality via the description of the character's appearance, home, job, etc.

Examples of Characterization:

1. The author wants you to understand that a character is evil, so he writes a scene in which the character wears all black, keeps voodoo dolls in his basement, and steals money from a charity for children.

2. The author wants you to understand that a child has heroic capabilities, so she describes how the child was able to lift a large rock and throw it, able to run faster than all of the children in the school, and had a "sixth sense" about danger.


Examples of Characterization from Literature and Film

1. In To Kill a Mockingbird, we learn that Scout is smart and perceptive for her age, but also sensitive when she goes to school able to read but the teacher is unhappy with her abilities and scolds her.

2. In The Hunger Games, we learn that Katniss is tender-hearted underneath all of her bravado-she takes her sister's place in the games and she refuses to kill Peeta.

3. In Harry Potter, Harry doesn't think he is anything special, so we learn a lot about Harry and how special he is to the battle between good and evil by how others react to him.

4. In Gone with the Wind, we learn that Scarlett has a strong will to survive when she is willing to marry Frank in order to save her family's plantation, "Tara."

Setting

Setting is a critical component to any short story that you may read. It works not only to show us where the story takes place, but also the mood of the story. Authors will use a variety of figurative language to create imagery in the story.

Endings

  1. Explicit ending – This is the ending that wraps everything up and answers all the questions. This ending will frequently tell what happens to each of the major characters, and is usually very satisfying in its completeness. Particularly well suited for novels (over short stories), when using this ending, it is especially important to watch for plot holes and missing clues. Example: Watership Down by Richard Adams.

  2. Implicit ending – If you like an ending that is strongly based on interpretation, then you like implicit endings. These endings are more common in short fiction. An example is The Nine Billion Names of God by Arthur C. Clark.

  3. Twist ending – As the name implies, this ending is unexpected or twisted. As a writer, everything you’ve led your reader to believe gets thrown out at the end, and is replaced by a new revelation when well done. If done poorly, your reader will feel cheated. The TV show The Twilight Zone was known for its twist endings.

  4. Tie-back ending – This ending ties the end of the story back to clues planted in the beginning. The example provided in the ending class is the short story entitled The Star by Arthur C. Clark, where the story opens with what the main character’s conflict is and ends with why.

  5. Unresolved ending – In unresolved endings, the main conflicts are left unanswered, such as in The Lady, or The Tiger by Frank R. Stockton. The reader is left to ponder the outcome. Cliffhanger endings would also fall under this category.

  6. Long view ending – These endings tell what happens to the characters a significant timeframe into the future. An example is Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows by J.K. Rowling, which ends telling who married whom, who had kids, etc. out into the future.

Conflict

 Conflict

  1. Person vs Self - "Person vs. Self" is the only true version of internal conflict you will find in literature. In this mode, the conflict takes place within the mind of the main character, and often involves the character making a decision between right and wrong, or other mixed emotions. However, this struggle could also exist in the form of a character battling mental illness. 

  1. Person vs. Person - "Person vs Person" is probably the most common form of external conflict, and is also known as interpersonal conflict. This mode lies at the heart of all dramatic arts and places the struggle directly between the protagonist and the antagonist -- otherwise known as the good guy and the bad guy. In a Person vs Person conflict, the protagonist wants something, and the antagonist obstructs the protagonist from getting what he wants. 

  1. Person vs. Society - This mode of external conflict occurs when the protagonist is placed at odds with a government or cultural tradition. This type of conflict applies to societal norms as well. For example, if a child gets in trouble with his parents for sneaking out of the house at night, he is in conflict with the societal tradition that children are expected to obey their parents.

  1. Person vs. Nature - "Person vs. Nature" pits the main character against the forces of nature -- in the form of a natural disaster or a similarly dangerous situation -- and is often associated with literary naturalism, which hinges on the idea that nature is indifferent to humanity. Stephen Crane's short story,  The Open Boat, is a prime example, and demonstrates that the sea can cause shipwrecks easily and without regard for humanity. 

  1. Person vs. Machine - "Person vs. Machine" can mean that a person is in direct combat with robots, in the context of science fiction, or it could mean simply that technology stands in the way of the protagonist getting what she wants. In the science-fiction version, the same attributes of a man vs. man conflict apply. However, if a person struggles to keep a job that a new machine can do better, the physical struggle is against the machine, but the emotional struggle is against the society that breeds technology. 

  1. Person vs. Fate/Supernatural - "Person vs. Fate" exists in any story in which the protagonist is struggling against a god or gods. It is sometimes considered part of "Person vs. Self" when focused on an internal, moral struggle, but should be considered separate in the context of epics -- such as The Iliad and  The Odyssey,  in which the gods are present antagonists. "Person vs. the Supernatural" falls into a similar standard: If the protagonist is the only one witnessing supernatural acts, it could be considered "Person vs. Self." However, if it's certain that these supernatural powers are real, then the mode of conflict stands on its own. 

About the Author: Hernando Téllez (22 March 1908 – 1966) was a Colombian journalist and author. Born and educated in Bogotá, Téllez entered very early the world of journalism, with which he is primarily identified, having been on the staff of some of Colombia's most popular newspapers and magazines. It was not until 1950 with the publication of his short story collection Cenizas para el viento (Ashes for the Wind), that his name became more widely known. His tragicomic tales evidence his keen and extremely sensitive observations of contemporary life and, more particularly, the anguishing reality of his native country.


During Téllez's lifetime, Colombia suffered through several civil wars and military dictatorships, collectively called La Violencia ("The Violence"). Téllez was also a student of history and was aware of the three rebellions of the 19th century which caused the former nation of Gran Colombia to be divided into the separate countries of Colombia, Venezuela and Ecuador. Téllez served in the Congress of Colombia.

Point of View

Point of View

Definitions: Point of View

  1. a particular attitude or way of considering a matter. Example: "I'm trying to get Matthew to change his point of view" 

  2. (In fictional writing) the narrator's position in relation to the story being told. Example: "This story is told from a child's point of view" 

  3. the position from which something or someone is observed. Example: "certain aspects are not visible from a single point of view"

Synonyms: opinion, view, belief, attitude, feeling, sentiment, thoughts; 

About the Author: Shirley Hardie Jackson (December 14, 1916 – August 8, 1965) was an American writer, known primarily for her works of horror and mystery. Over the duration of her writing career, which spanned over two decades, she composed six novels, two memoirs, and over 200 short stories.


After publishing her debut novel The Road Through the Wall (1948), a semi-autobiographical account of her childhood in California, Jackson gained significant public attention for her short story "The Lottery," which details a secret, sinister underside to a bucolic American village. She continued to publish numerous short stories in literary journals and magazines throughout the 1950s, some of which were assembled and reissued in her 1953 memoir Life Among the Savages. In 1959, she published The Haunting of Hill House, a supernatural horror novel widely considered to be one of the best ghost stories ever written.

Literary Devices

Writers use a range of techniques and devices to create the effects they’re after. Some of these devices are used principally by poets, whereas others are common to writers of both prose and poetry.

Imagery

You can have experience only through your five senses: you can see, hear, feel, taste, and smell. When writers want to share their experiences, they try to appeal to the senses by describing how something looks, sounds, feels, tastes, or smells. Sensory details are the specific words that appeal to your senses to support the dominant impression of a description.

An image is a word picture that is created by using vivid sensory details. Writing that creates images in the minds of readers is said to contain imagery. When writers use imagery, their words make you feel as though you can see, smell, touch, hear, or even taste what they’re describing. Here are examples of writing that appeals to each sense:

Sight: sparkling diamond

Hearing: shrieking siren

Taste: salty, buttered popcorn

Smell: rotten eggs

Touch: slimy slug

It’s easy to see that imagery uses colourful, specific words to create a picture in the reader’s mind. Sensory details must be very specific words in order to create effective images. The sentence, “The dog made a noise,” doesn’t give the reader a very clear picture. However, the sentence, “The panting, struggling German shepherd whimpered in his agony,” creates a more effective image. Not only do you see and hear the dog, but you also get the impression of suffering.

Figurative Language

Here are two statements that say approximately the same thing:

Try to do great things .

Hitch your wagon to a star.

Although both statements have the same meaning, one is more interesting than the other. The first one makes a straightforward statement; it uses literal language. The second example, on the other hand, encourages you to use your imagination to create a special image. It uses figurative language.

Figurative language is effective because it adds vividness to a description. It also gives concreteness, beauty, and humour to words and ideas. Figurative language contributes to the mood or theme of a poem or passage.

Figures of Speech

Figures of speech are some of the tools a writer uses to create imagery. For example, “rough as sandpaper” very effectively appeals to the sense of touch. “Diamond-studded sky” creates a visual image more effectively than the phrase “many stars in the sky.”

Four common figures of speech are similes, metaphors, personification, and hyperbole.

The Simile

A good way to increase the effectiveness of a word picture or image is to compare an object or person to something else. This comparison can be a forceful tool in both writing and speaking. A simile is a comparison introduced by the word like or as.

The frisky puppy was as wiggly as an eel.

Leaves drifted in the gentle wind like tiny parachutes.

Notice that in these examples the two things compared in each sentence are unlike in most ways, but appear to be alike in one important aspect. This unusual comparison is what makes a simile striking.

The Metaphor

A metaphor is another type of comparison that’s used frequently in prose and poetry. A metaphor, like a simile, makes a comparison, but it doesn’t use the words like or as.

On their shining tracks, the waiting diesel engines were crouching cats, purring softly.

The ripe pumpkins were golden idols among the corn stalks.

In these examples, one thing is described as if it were something else. The diesel engines were purring cats, and the pumpkins were golden idols.

Once you can recognize metaphors in poetry and prose, you’ll be able to appreciate their effectiveness in language. Sometimes a writer uses a metaphorical comparison over an entire poem or written work. This extended metaphor is often easier to recognize because it is developed over the entire piece of writing, and it then becomes more obvious. In the next example, the author compares clouds to several things:

I remember once, as a kid, lying on my back watching clouds. Row upon row of factory-perfect models drifted along the assembly line. There went a nifty schooner, flag flying — and look, a snapping toy poodle with the most absurd cut! Next came chilly Greenland, with Labrador much too close for comfort. But the banana split was the best one of all.

Personification

Personification is the giving of human characteristics, powers, or feelings to something non-human. Personification is really a type of metaphor in which the comparison is always made to a human being:

The telephone poles marched along the highway as far as the eye could see .

The waters of the brook chuckled as they passed us on their way.

In the first of these examples, the telephone poles are being compared to soldiers as they march, standing straight and evenly spaced, along the road. In the second example, the waters in the brook are compared to chuckling, happy people — children perhaps.

Hyperbole

Hyperbole is an extravagant exaggeration, usually used for comic or dramatic effect:

The story would burn your ears off if I told you.

The story wouldn’t really burn off your ears, but this exaggeration helps to emphasize what’s being said. Hyperbole is intentional exaggeration used to emphasize an idea.

Here are two more examples of hyperbole — ones you’ve probably heard many times:

It was so funny I split my sides laughing.

I simply died of embarrassment.

Irony

Irony has a wide range of meanings. At its simplest, irony is a form of expression that implies something different or even opposite to what is actually said, as in this example:

So you broke your arm the day of the big game! That's just great.

Irony of this sort, when a person says the opposite of what he or she means, is called verbal irony.

Another kind of irony occurs when something turns out in an opposite way to what is expected. Suppose that a team has played splendidly all year but, in the final game, plays very badly and suffers a humiliating defeat. This strange twist, which often occurs with events, is called irony of situation.

In literature, the tme meaning of a set of circumstances often isn’t revealed until the outcome of the circumstances is seen; then a contradiction in the expected outcome is the result. The situation may seem to be developing to its logical conclusion, yet almost at the end it takes an opposite turn. This unexpected, or unintended, development is an example of irony of situation.

In the short story, “The Gift of the Magi,” by O. Henry, Della sells her beautiful long hair in order to buy her husband, Jim, a watch chain. Meanwhile, Jim pawns his cherished watch to buy Della a present of hair combs. This ironic twist of fate produces a conclusion that, to both characters and readers, is entirely unexpected.

Satire

Satire is a form of writing in which the writer criticizes or ridicules something, such as society, institutions, politics, religion, or education. However, it isn’t direct criticism. Satire often describes a completely different situation, but makes indirect parallels and references to things you know so that you realize what the writer is criticizing.

In one very famous satirical work, the writer Jonathan Swift wrote an essay in which he suggested that the poor people of his country should sell their children to the rich as a source of food. Of course, his point was to criticize his society, in which some people lived in such grinding poverty that they found it very difficult to feed and clothe themselves and their children, whereas others in society had much more than they needed and refused to share their wealth. In his satirical essay. Swift suggested that since the rich were taking everything else from the poor anyway, they might as well take their children. Readers who missed Swift’s satire were horrified by his proposal.

Very often writers use satire to achieve humour in their writing. In fact, to be effective, satire must be humorous; it should have sharpness, but it shouldn’t be bitter and caustic. It scores its point without causing hurt. Good satire is often subtle, sometimes so subtle that some people misunderstand it.

Symbolism

A symbol is something that stands for something else. It can be a word, a person, an action, or an object that takes on a meaning far beyond its ordinary meaning. For example, the dove and the olive branch are symbols of peace. The fist is a symbol of aggression.

A symbol is more than a sign. A sign brings to mind a single meaning; a symbol brings to mind a more complex idea that signals both mind and emotion. For example, the Canadian maple leaf is a symbol; it represents a cluster of ideas, attitudes, and feelings.

A literary symbol is an object, a situation, or an action that has a literal meaning within a story or poem, but suggests other meanings as well. For example, darkness might symbolize ignorance or depression, while dawn might mean a new beginning.

Don’t fall into the trap, however, of assuming that a literary symbol must always mean the same thing. For example, the Sun often symbolizes life, but a writer might use it as a symbol of power or dominance or something entirely different. Always let the story or poem itself alert you to what a symbol means.

Allusion

An allusion is an indirect reference to something or someone generally familiar. Many allusions are to historical or mythological figures. For example, “He’s as old as Methuselah” is an allusion to a man who’s said to have lived 969 years. Of course, if the reader doesn’t know of Methuselah, the allusion is meaningless. The allusion then becomes a barrier to communication.

If writers want to get their message across to readers, they must be aware of possible barriers and write specifically for a group of readers. Readers, on the other hand, must also be aware of these barriers and take steps to remove as many as possible. The more you read and learn, the more allusions you’ll be able to recognize. You can also use a dictionary to help you discover the meaning of many allusions.

Flashback

Flashback is a common technique for revealing something important that happened in the past. The readers or viewers, typically, are involved in the present action when suddenly the writer takes them back to the past for a while. This return to the past is sometimes done as a memory.

An author may signal a flashback in different ways. Occasionally, an author will leave additional space between the part of the story in the current time and the flashback. Some authors change the font to emphasize a flashback.

Most of the time, an author signals a flashback with words. A verb tense shift from the present to the past tense may be used:

I remember the night so clearly. I had gone upstairs to change for the party. Suddenly, I heard a scream outside my window....

Foreshadowing

Foreshadowing occurs when the author gives hints or clues about what’s going to happen. Sometimes the hints are so subtle that you may miss them until the event has occurred. Upon rereading the story, however, you’ll find foreshadowing more obvious. This technique adds interest and suspense as you wait for what you’re subtly warned about to happen:

As I walked past the graveyard that foggy night, I felt that someone was watching me. Yet, when I turned around, no one was there .

I should have known that Marco could not be trusted.

Although these examples are somewhat obvious, not all foreshadowing is this simple. A writer will often leave subtle clues for the reader: a particular brand of cough drops, a peculiar habit, a way of speaking, an odd noise, a strange glance. It takes a discerning reader to become aware of these hints.

Alliteration

Alliteration is the repeated use of an initial consonant sound in two or more words in close proximity (the same line or nearby lines). This sound device contributes to the melody of the writing. Writers often use alliteration to gain attention, to bind phrases together, or to create a musical effect.

In this line by Edgar Allan Poe from his poem “The Bells,” the t sound is emphasized:

What a tale of terror, now, their turbulency tells!

Here’s another example of alliteration from Tennyson’s “The Eagle”:

He clasps the crag with crooked hands;

Onomatopoeia

Onomatopoeia or imitative harmony is the use of words whose sound suggests their meaning:

swish buzz bubble drip crash hum hiss plop bang whir

When Alfred Noyes wanted to show the sound of a horse in his poem “The Highwayman,” he used the following words:

Over the cobbles he clattered and clashed in the dark inn-yard

Later in the poem, Noyes uses onomatopoeia again:

Tlot-tlot; tlot-tlot! Had they heard it? The horse-hoofs ringing clear;

Sometimes a poem will use an entire line or even a stanza of imitative words to convey a special effect, as in these lines from Shakespeare’s Macbeth:

Double, double, toil and trouble;

Fire burn, and cauldron bubble.

Repetition

Poets, along with other writers, frequently repeat words or phrases to emphasize them or to create a rhythmic effect. Here’s an example from the poem “The Highwayman” by Alfred Noyes:

And the highwayman came riding —

Riding — riding —

The highwayman came riding, up to the old inn-door.

Annotating Readings

Annotate important passages as you read. Record questions, patterns, unfamiliar words, and details that may become useful evidence.

Example of Annotations

If you would like some assistance when you annotate your readings, please let your teacher know.

Lesson 5: Writing a Short Story Analysis

Writing a Short Story Analysis

When you write a short story analysis, you are writing a response that analyzes the story you have read. 

Remember:

  • you are providing an opinion as to the value of the work. 
  • Your response should use the terminology of the short story. 
  • You need to discuss the major elements, including, but not limited to, the plot, setting, characters, point of view and theme. 

Suggested Format

Introduction

  • The response needs to have an introduction which identifies the title and author, as well as make a general comment about the story as a whole.

Paragraph 1

  • should briefly retell the plot of the story. 

Paragraph 2

  • should discuss the effectiveness of the plot and setting, including specific details from the story. 

Paragraph 3

  • should discuss the characters and point of view, once again providing support from the story. 

Paragraph 4

  • should indicate the theme, based on how the author develops and, most importantly, ends, the story. 

Conclusion

  • A final brief concluding paragraph should finish the response by providing a recommendation as to who would find this story interesting. 

Use the Short Story Bank to read the assigned text. Then use Short Story Questions and the Writing Studio to develop your analysis.
